notes:
Need to search first.These are my notes on Psalm 127. I found good verse-by-verse material from the older commentaries, Enduring Word and Augustine. The one clear disagreement among Protestants is over verses 3–5 and birth control. I didn't find anything on several of the sites you asked for; those gaps are listed at the end.

---

## Title / v. 1

**Who wrote it?**
- Matthew Henry reads the title as "for Solomon." On this view David wrote it for Solomon, who had a house to build, a city to keep and a family line to raise, and was teaching him to depend on God's providence. Henry also notes that others take it as Solomon's own song and compare it with Ecclesiastes, since both show how empty worldly anxiety is. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_127.cfm
- Gill links the psalm to David's preparations for the temple and the promise that success depended on the Lord (1 Chronicles 28:20). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-127.html
- The Syriac title calls it a psalm of David about Solomon, and also connects it with Haggai and Zechariah, who pushed forward the rebuilding of the temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/127-1.html

**What "house" means**
- Ellicott says the house is any house, not the temple. Even in ordinary work, it is God's blessing that brings success. https://biblehub.com/psalms/127-1.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary likewise reads "a house" and "a city," meaning any house or city at all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/127.htm
- Guzik (Enduring Word) thinks "house" may also mean a family. Citing Clarke, he notes that the Hebrew words for son, daughter and house all come from the root "to build." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-127/
- Clarke lists three biblical senses of "building a house": building the temple, building an ordinary dwelling, and having many descendants. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/127-1.html
- Against this, the Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary argues that pairing "house" with "city" shows a literal building is meant. It suggests Solomon may have been building his palace and the temple at the time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-127.html

**Main point: work, but don't trust in your work**
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik) says the psalm doesn't tell builders to stop building or watchmen to stop watching. It assumes they will do their best, but forbids them to trust in what they have done. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-127/
- Guzik also notes that Edinburgh's motto, *Nisi Dominus Frustra*, comes from this verse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-127/
- Ellicott pictures a house built with great effort, or a carefully planned city, falling to a night attack despite the strictest guard, unless God's providence protects it. https://biblehub.com/psalms/127-1.htm
- Maclaren (Expositor's Bible) points out that the psalmist uses past tenses, as if showing us the failure afterwards: a half-built house in ruins, a city sacked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/127.htm

**Reading it about the church**
- Augustine (Catholic, Church Fathers) says Christ is the true Solomon, the true Peacemaker, and builds his own house, the church. The builders are those who preach God's word. The watchmen are pastors and bishops, who can only guard people as far as human beings are able. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801127.htm
- He also says preachers speak from outside, while God builds within. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.CXXVII.html
- The Biblical Illustrator applies the house to the home, business, character, nation and church, but insists God's keeping doesn't rule out human effort: we must watch even though God keeps us. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-127.html

## v. 2

**What is condemned**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the target is being anxious and troubled over your work, and making your life a burden by living on worry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/127.htm
- Barnes says the psalmist is not condemning early rising. His point is that even when you work hard, you still depend on God. Barnes suggests "bread of sorrows" may echo the curse on Adam's work (Genesis 3:17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/127-2.htm
- The Geneva Study Bible's note says God does not excuse his people from labour; he makes their labour comfortable, almost like rest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/127-2.htm
- Guzik points out that Solomon's Proverbs praise the hard worker. What is in view here is trusting in our own effort and the anxiety that comes with it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-127/

**"He gives his beloved sleep": is sleep the gift, or does God give while they sleep?** Commentators really do differ here.
- Ellicott thinks "in sleep / while they sleep" fits the context best: God gives his beloved, as they sleep, what others toil for in vain (compare Proverbs 10:22 and Mark 4:27). He admits the familiar reading, with sleep itself as God's gift, is "equally true and equally beautiful." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/127-2.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary also reads "giveth to his beloved in sleep," comparing Matthew 6:25–34. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/127.htm
- Maclaren says the familiar King James rendering, though much loved, has to go. The contrast is between useless toil and God giving his beloved what that toil was aiming for, while they sleep. He adds that this is no preaching of laziness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/127.htm
- Barnes takes the other side. He rejects "rest without toil" and "gifts in sleep" as unlikely, and says the meaning is a calm, trusting mind that lets God's people sleep while others lie awake worrying. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/127-2.htm
- Matthew Henry takes it as both bodily sleep and contentment of mind. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_127.cfm
- Benson says God gives quiet rest of body and mind. If some of our time goes to prayer rather than all of it to prayerless worry, we can lie down at night with confidence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/127-2.htm

**Who is "his beloved"?**
- Poole hears an allusion to Solomon's other name, Jedidiah, "beloved of the Lord" (2 Samuel 12:25). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/127-2.htm
- Boice (quoted by Guzik) says the same. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-127/
- Gill goes further and applies it to Christ, the Father's beloved, resting in the grave; to believers falling asleep in Jesus at death; and to eternal rest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/127-2.htm
- The Pulpit homilies likewise extend it to the "sleep of death" for those who die in the Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/127.htm

**Popular use**
- Guzik applies the verse devotionally. He recommends that believers troubled by bad dreams claim it as a promise. https://enduringword.com/ask-me-anything-qa-for-september-2-2021/

## v. 3

- **Why children come next:** the Pulpit Commentary says children are plainly God's free gift, and one way he rewards the faithful (Deuteronomy 28). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/127.htm
- **"Reward" is grace, not wages:** Benson and Poole both say this is a reward of grace, not something good people have earned (Romans 4:4). Barnes argues "his reward" misleads; the sense is a blessing with which God favours his people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/127-3.htm
- **Children are not chance:** the commentary quoted on CCEL's study page (the part I saw doesn't name its author) says the word for "reward" covers whatever God gives. Children are not chance; God hands them out as he sees fit. https://www.ccel.org/study/Psalm_127:3
- **Not a burden:** Spurgeon (via Guzik) says God gives children as a favour, not as a penalty or a burden. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-127/
- **Solomon's irony:** Guzik notes the irony that Solomon, with 700 wives and 300 concubines, has only one descendant we know of. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-127/
- **Spiritual children:** Gill applies the verse to believers as the Father's gift to Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/127-3.htm

## v. 4

- **"Children born in one's youth":** the Pulpit Commentary says these are children born while the father is young. They will protect him in old age the way arrows protect a warrior. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/127.htm
- Matthew Henry offers this, or alternatively children who are themselves still young. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_127.cfm
- **Shaping the arrow:** Henry says children "in the hand" can be aimed at God's glory. Once they go out into the world, they are arrows out of the hand and it is too late to bend them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_127.cfm
- Trapp (quoted by Guzik) says arrows are made by skill, not by growing. Children's natures likewise need shaping by grace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-127/
- **Augustine's reading:** the arrows are the apostles, shot by Christ's mighty arm to the ends of the earth. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801127.htm

## v. 5

**The traditional reading**
- The Pulpit Commentary says "the gate" was where court cases were heard. A man with several strong sons on his side would have the advantage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/127.htm
- Maclaren thinks real warfare is unlikely. The setting is everyday disputes with neighbours. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/127.htm

**"They" or "he"?** Ellicott says "they" does not mean the sons; Hebrew poetry often switches between singular and plural. https://biblehub.com/psalms/127-5.htm Gill notes that Aben Ezra takes it as father and children together, though Gill himself thinks the parents are meant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/127-5.htm

**Less common readings**
- Clarke suggests the "quiver" is the wife, so the blessing is a fruitful wife. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/psalms/127-5.html
- Gill reports that the Jewish commentator Jarchi took the children as disciples of the wise. Gill also applies the verse to young converts. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/psalms/127-5.html

**Real Protestant disagreement: large families and birth control**
- Got Questions describes the Quiverfull movement, which rejects all birth control and accepts as many children as God gives, based on this verse. It argues this takes "quiver full" out of context and is no blanket command. https://www.gotquestions.org/quiver-full-of-children.html
- Desiring God (Baptist) says any attitude that doesn't see children as a good gift is wrong. But God has not given everyone the same size quiver, so birth control can be used wisely. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/does-the-bible-permit-birth-control
- Bible.org takes a similar line. https://bible.org/question/what-does-bible-say-about-birth-control
- A Bible Hub article is more sympathetic to Quiverfull. https://biblehub.com/q/bible's_view_on_quiverfull,_patriarchy.htm
- Spurgeon takes a gentler line: a small quiver can still be full, and a man's life doesn't consist in how many children he has. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-127/

---

**What I couldn't find:** I didn't get to the NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, catholic.com, oca.org, or any Lutheran, Methodist-site or Pentecostal-site pages on this psalm. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on it. The only Catholic material is Augustine's reading, which is about Christ and the church. I don't have a Catholic teaching on birth control drawn from this psalm. I ran out of searches before I could check these sources.
